analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 0.25% excise tax on over-the-counter derivatives transactions to make them reportable.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: after being referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2009, it saw no action and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a small tax — 0.25% of the value of the deal — to every derivative transaction traded privately off exchanges rather than on public markets. It covers options, forward contracts, short positions, credit default swaps and similar instruments. To collect the tax, traders would have to file annual returns describing each deal, the parties, the underlying asset, and how it settles — creating a paper trail on a market that is largely hidden today. The Treasury would also have to report to Congress on the size and nature of these markets and whether they should be regulated.
analysis.who_benefits: The public gains a transparency record: a market that contributed to the 2008 crisis — private derivatives trades like credit default swaps — would have to be described on tax returns, giving regulators and Congress their first detailed statistical picture of it. The tax would also raise revenue from high-volume financial trading.

how_it_helps.text: Each party to a covered off-exchange derivative deal would owe 0.25% of the deal's notional value, with both parties jointly liable for payment. [S3]

To comply, traders must file annual returns describing the instrument, the parties and their tax residences, the deal's value, the underlying asset, and any physical settlement terms — a detailed record of a market that currently trades in the dark. [S3]
The Treasury Secretary must report to Congress with statistical analysis of the market and a detailed assessment of whether and how the over-the-counter derivatives market should be regulated. [S3]
The tax applies only to trades not made on a qualified exchange, so it targets the private, opaque corner of the derivatives market while leaving exchange-traded trades alone. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Banks, hedge funds, and other dealers who trade derivatives privately off exchanges would pay the tax and bear new reporting costs. Some of that cost would likely be passed into prices for businesses and investors who use derivatives to hedge — for example, companies locking in fuel or crop prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Off-exchange derivatives traders, banks and hedge funds

drawbacks.text: A 0.25% tax on notional value is large relative to typical derivatives trading costs, and it applies to every covered transaction — including legitimate hedging by airlines, farmers, and manufacturers that manage real business risk through private contracts, not just speculation. [S3]
Both parties to a deal are jointly and severally liable, which could create legal disputes over tax responsibility in complex multi-party transactions. [S3]

The bill does not designate the revenue for any specific public purpose; it is simply a new tax, and Treasury could exclude or include transactions by regulation, leaving the scope partly to future decisions. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency goal was real and valuable after a crisis caused in part by opaque private derivatives trades. But the tax as written is blunt: taxing notional value at 0.25% falls on routine hedging, not just risky speculation, and could raise costs for ordinary businesses. A more targeted design might have required disclosure without the broad tax. Still, the bill was a serious attempt to shine light on a market that had resisted it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it quietly expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson of Connecticut introduced the Transparent Markets Act of 2009 on July 9, 2009. [S1] [S3]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day. [S5]
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on. [S4]
No committee vote, markup, or floor action is recorded; the bill's action history ends with the referral. [S5]
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011, never receiving a vote in either chamber. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Off-exchange derivatives dealers — the banks and trading firms whose private transactions would have been taxed and documented — are better off, since they avoided both the tax and the disclosure. The Ways and Means Committee never had to take a position.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, proposing a 0.25% tax and mandatory disclosure on off-exchange derivatives trades.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: After the bill was referred to his committee, no markup, vote, or further action was ever scheduled on it. [S5]

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so the partisan split on the merits is unknown; the bill drew only one cosponsor from the Democratic majority and none from Republicans. [S4]

industries.industry: Over-the-counter derivatives dealers (banks, hedge funds, broker-dealers)
industries.note: Dealers in privately negotiated derivatives — credit default swaps, forwards, options — would have paid a 0.25% tax on notional value and had to disclose every trade on annual tax returns. Their interest lay in keeping this market untaxed and undocumented, the opposite of the public's interest in transparency after the 2008 crisis. [S3]

industries.industry: Businesses using derivatives to hedge risk
industries.note: Companies that privately hedge fuel, crops, or interest rates through off-exchange contracts would have faced the tax on routine hedging. Some costs would likely have been passed to consumers. [S3]

industries.industry: On-exchange markets (regulated futures and securities exchanges)
industries.note: Because the tax applies only to trades not made on a qualified exchange, it would have pushed trading onto public exchanges, where prices and volumes are visible to everyone. [S3]
